Learning outcomes

By the end of Lecture B you should be able to:

  1. Explain the bias-variance decomposition of expected test error.
  2. State the tradeoff and connect it to the U-curve.
  3. Derive and apply ridge regression, and tune \lambda by CV.
  4. Connect ridge to the Module 1 uniqueness condition.

Speaker note: 2A found the U empirically; 2B explains it (bias-variance) and gives a knob to move along it (ridge).

Recap: the U, and why

Lecture A: test error is U-shaped in complexity — underfit on the left, overfit on the right.

Cross-validation told us where the bottom is. Now: why is there a U at all?

Speaker note: one line back to 2A. The U is not an accident — it is the sum of two competing quantities. Name them next.

Bias and variance, intuitively

Imagine refitting on many datasets drawn the same way:

  • Bias — the systematic miss: even on average, a too-simple model can’t reach the truth.
  • Variance — the sensitivity: a too-flexible model swings wildly from one dataset to the next.

Speaker note: this is the prediction-space view of the SAME repeated-sampling story the Module 3 covariance-ellipse tool shows in parameter space — flag the resonance. There, spread of ŵ; here, spread of the fitted curve.

Bias and variance on the data

Figure 1: Repeated fits: degree 1 (biased, tight) vs. degree 9 (low-bias, high-variance).

The decomposition

For a fixed input \mathbf{x}, expected test error splits into three pieces:

\mathbb{E}\bigl[(y - \hat{f}(\mathbf{x}))^2\bigr] \;=\; \underbrace{\text{bias}^2}_{\text{systematic}} \;+\; \underbrace{\text{variance}}_{\text{sensitivity}} \;+\; \underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{irreducible}} .

The \sigma^2 floor is noise no model can beat. Full derivation → appendix-bias-variance.html.

Speaker note: expectation over training sets, at a fixed \mathbf{x}. The irreducible term is why even the true model has nonzero test error.

The tradeoff

As complexity rises:

  • bias^2 falls — the model can represent more;
  • variance rises — the model chases the sample;
  • their sum is the U, resting on the irreducible \sigma^2 floor.

The best model is not the most flexible one — it is the one that balances the two.

Speaker note: the U from 2A = bias² + variance (+ σ²). Underfit = bias-dominated (left); overfit = variance-dominated (right). Regularization moves us left.

Controlling the tradeoff: regularization.

Ridge regression

Add a penalty on the size of the weights:

\mathcal{L}_{\text{ridge}}(\mathbf{w}) = \lVert \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}\rVert_2^2 + \lambda\lVert \mathbf{w}\rVert_2^2 .

(The intercept w_0 is not penalized — the code centers instead. We also drop the 1/N here; it only rescales \lambda.)

  • \lambda = 0 → ordinary least squares.
  • \lambda > 0 → shrinks weights toward \mathbf{0}, trading a little bias for less variance.

Speaker note: the penalty discourages large, wiggly-curve coefficients. λ is the knob that moves us along the bias-variance U — tuned by CV (2A).

Ridge: the closed form

The penalty just adds \lambda\mathbf{I} inside the normal equations:

\boxed{\;\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{\text{ridge}} = \left(\mathbf{X}^{\!\top}\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{X}^{\!\top}\mathbf{y}\;}

\mathbf{X}^{\!\top}\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I} is positive definite for any \lambda>0 — so it is always invertible. Ridge guarantees the unique solution that Module 1 needed full column rank for.

Speaker note: through-line node. In M1, uniqueness required \mathbf{X}^{\!\top}\mathbf{X} invertible (full column rank). Ridge adds \lambda\mathbf{I}, lifting every eigenvalue by λ>0 — invertibility for free, even when N<D or columns collide.

The coefficient path

Figure 2: Ridge shrinks every coefficient toward 0 as λ grows (log-λ axis).

The two limits

  • \lambda \to 0: the penalty vanishes — ridge recovers OLS (\hat{\mathbf{w}} from Module 1). Maximum variance, minimum bias.
  • \lambda \to \infty: the penalty dominates — \hat{\mathbf{w}} \to \mathbf{0}, the model predicts a constant. Maximum bias, minimum variance.

The useful \lambda lives in between — found by cross-validation.

Speaker note: both ends are degenerate. λ→0 is the overfit right end of the U; λ→∞ is the underfit left end. CV picks the middle.

Choosing λ by cross-validation

Figure 3: 5-fold CV error vs. λ for a degree-14 ridge fit; the minimum is the CV choice.

Forward hook

The ridge penalty \lambda\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_2^2 is secretly a Gaussian prior on \mathbf{w}: ridge is MAP estimation under that prior. We derive that in Module 4.

So “shrink the weights” and “believe, a priori, the weights are small” are the same statement — one more object doing double duty across the term.

Speaker note: plant this now. In M4, the Gaussian prior + Gaussian likelihood gives a posterior whose mode is exactly ŵ_ridge with λ = σ²/τ². Regularization = prior.

Recap

  • Bias-variance — test error = bias^2 + variance +\ \sigma^2; the U is their sum.
  • Ridge — \mathcal{L}+\lambda\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2, closed form \hat{\mathbf{w}}_{\text{ridge}}=(\mathbf{X}^{\!\top}\mathbf{X}+\lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^{\!\top}\mathbf{y}; always invertible (intercept not penalized; the dropped 1/N only rescales \lambda).
  • Tune \lambda by CV — the knob that balances the tradeoff.

Module 2 has no standalone checkpoint; generalization discipline is assessed through your modeling choices in Part 1.

Speaker note: bias-variance is the why, ridge is the control, CV is the tuner. Carry the ridge-as-prior hook into Module 4.
